title: Two Italians killed in strike in Kuwait, as Iran denies responsibility
summary: The pair were technicians for German company Rheinmetall, according to Italy's foreign ministry.
text:
Two Italians killed in strike in Kuwait, as Iran denies responsibility
- Published
Two Italian nationals have died following a strike on a facility in Kuwait which both countries have blamed on Iran.
The pair were technicians working for German arms manufacturing company Rheinmetall, Italy's foreign ministry said.
Iran has denied responsibility for the attack, with armed forces spokesperson Abolfazl Shekarchi saying "no military or offensive operations have been conducted" by its military.
Kuwait's defence ministry said earlier that four people - the two Italians, a Kuwaiti national and Pakistani national - had been injured from falling shrapnel after a number of drones from Iran were detected and intercepted.
It comes just over a week after Kuwait said it had repelled overnight Iranian drone attacks on an airbase which hosts US forces - the first strikes in more than two months on the country.
Recent exchanges of fire between the US and Iran, and a deadlock in negotiations, have raised fears of a major escalation in the war.
The conflict began when US and Israel attacked Iran in late February, with Iran retaliating by launching missiles and drones at Israel and Gulf Arab states hosting US military assets and personnel.
Iranian-backed militias in the region have also carried out attacks on the US's Gulf allies.
Kuwait's Army said the latest attack was on a "vital site in the country" and was the result of "heinous Iranian aggression", while confirming the deaths of the two Italian nationals.
Meanwhile, Italy's foreign ministry said in a statement: "An explosion caused by a drone attack... occurred at a site where two Italian technicians from the company Rheinmetall Italia were working."
The two Italian nationals were working at an air defence detection station and performing maintenance work on systems used by the Kuwaiti Armed Forces, according to Italian press agency Ansa, citing Italy's foreign ministry.
Italian media outlets have named the two individuals. One of the men was reported to be 36, while the other was 65 and nearing retirement.
Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni wrote on X: "On my own behalf and on behalf of the government, I express my deepest sympathy and offer my heartfelt condolences to the victims' families.
"My thoughts are with all those affected by the attack and their families."
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen wrote on social media: "We must step up pressure on Iran to end these unacceptable attacks against its neighbours and our partners in the Gulf.
"Today's events are a further reminder that security in the Gulf is a security issue for us all."

title: Watch: Roofs torn off and streets under water as severe weather hits US
summary: Hundreds of thousands have been affected by storms in the country as the Thanksgiving holiday weekend begins.
text:
Watch: Roofs torn off and streets under water as severe weather hits US
Powerful storms are battering both US coasts as the Thanksgiving holiday weekend gets under way.
Hundreds of flights have been cancelled and hundreds of thousands are without power, in states including Virginia, North Carolina and New Jersey.
Strong winds have blown roofs off houses and floodwater has submerged streets.

title: Congo Ebola outbreak reaches 12,000 cases as some responders evacuate
summary: As the fast-moving outbreak continues to spread in eastern Congo, fighting between rebels and the army is disrupting efforts to contain the spread of the disease.
text:
Congo Ebola outbreak reaches 12,000 cases as some responders evacuate
BUNIA, Congo — The fast-moving Ebola outbreak in eastern Congo has topped 12,000 confirmed cases, government data showed Thursday, as fighting between rebels and the army disrupts efforts to contain the spread of the disease.
It is the fastest-growing Ebola outbreak in history and nearly half the 12,021 people confirmed to have the virus have died, according to data from Congo's Ministry of Health. It is also the deadliest of Congo's 17 outbreaks and is on track to surpass the death toll from the West African outbreak that killed 11,000 people between 2014 and 2016.
The outbreak declared in May is caused by the rare Bundibugyo virus, for which there is no approved vaccine or treatment. Response teams are battling armed conflict, poor roads and violence from residents fueled by mistrust and misinformation.
Ebola spreads through direct contact with the blood or other bodily fluids of people who are sick or have died from the disease. Containing the disease requires quickly identifying and treating patients in isolation, monitoring people who may have been exposed and safely burying the dead.
Fighting between the army and the Convention pour la révolution populaire rebels resumed Thursday morning in Iga-Barrière, a mining town about 25 kilometers (15 miles) north of Bunia in eastern Congo, sending new waves of displaced people toward the city. Bunia is the capital of northeastern Ituri province and a major hub for the Ebola response.
CRP is one of more than 100 armed groups in eastern Congo, where conflict has created one of the world's most severe humanitarian crises. The group was founded last year by former warlord Thomas Lubanga, who was convicted by the International Criminal Court in 2012 of recruiting children under 15 and using them in fighting.
Fighting between the army and the rebels earlier this week had already prevented teams from reaching some communities, disrupted monitoring of people exposed to the virus and left some treatment centers with fewer staff, Dr. Catherine Smallwood, the World Health Organization's Ebola incident manager, said Wednesday.
Smallwood said that about a dozen people, including two WHO personnel and Congolese health officials, were evacuated to Bunia on Tuesday after three full days trapped in a hospital in Akwe, northeast of the provincial capital, amid intense crossfire.

title: Nine injured, three critically, after Bangkok oil refinery explosion
summary: Black smoke could be seen across Bangkok's skyline after the blast, as officials urged residents to leave the area.
text:
Nine injured, three critically, after Bangkok oil refinery explosion
- Published
Nine people have been injured after an explosion at an oil refinery in Bangkok, authorities have said.
Three of them are in critical condition, according to news agency AFP, which said the local hospital had revised its earlier assessment of four.
A fire broke out after the blast at the Phra Khanong facility run by energy giant Bangchak Corporation in the east of Thailand's capital at around 14:45 (07:45 GMT).
The company said the fire was brought under control and put out within 30 minutes, adding that the cause of the incident was being investigated.
Black smoke could be seen across Bangkok's skyline after the blast, as local officials told residents to leave the area.
An alert sent to mobile phones by Bangkok authorities confirmed that the fire was under control, but urged people to avoid the area.
Eyewitnesses shared video clips on social media of flames and smoke rising above the refinery.
On a visit to the scene, Thailand's energy minister Akanat Promphan said it appeared the impact of the explosion was limited because the fire started in a distillation tower about 100m (330ft) from where oil was being stored.
He said the incident was concerning as the refinery was in a residential area and the government was suspending production until it could be confident that operations would resume without any issues.
Bangchak Corporation said air quality monitoring in the immediate area around the refinery was within normal ranges.
It confirmed that production at the site, which can process up to 120,000 barrels of oil a day had been shut down. The company has a second refinery in Chonburi province, about 50 miles (80km) from Bangkok, handling a daily capacity of about 180,000 barrels.
An explosion occurred at the Bangkok refinery in July 2012, sparking a fire but no reported injuries.

title: North Korea's Kim vows to build more nuclear weapons after ignoring Trump's overture
summary: Leader Kim Jong Un reportedly visited facilities that produce nuclear ingredients and called for building more nuclear weapons to cope with threats from the U.S. and South Korea.
text:
North Korea's Kim vows to build more nuclear weapons after ignoring Trump's overture
SEOUL, South Korea — North Korean leader Kim Jong Un visited facilities that produce nuclear ingredients and called for building more nuclear weapons, days after ignoring U.S. President Donald Trump's offer to meet during his recent visit to Asia.
Experts say Kim likely wants to show off his evolving nuclear arsenal, the backbone of his authoritarian rule, and reaffirm his rejection of any future talks on dismantling his nuclear program.
The North's official Korean Central News Agency said Thursday that Kim inspected two nuclear materials production factories, one newly inaugurated and the other being expanded. KCNA photos showed Kim and senior military officials walking between dense rows of what appeared to be centrifuges used to produce weapons-grade uranium and touring halls displaying what were believed to be warheads. Some of the images were blurred.
KCNA said Kim visited a nuclear-powered equipment production base and a nuclear research institute as well on Wednesday.
North Korea has disclosed a uranium enrichment site a few times since it showed one at its main Yongbyon nuclear complex to visiting American scholars in 2010. North Korea didn't say where the nuclear materials production factories that Kim visited this week are located. In June, when North Korea disclosed parts of a uranium enrichment site while reporting on Kim's visit there, outside experts assessed it was likely an additional uranium enrichment facility at Yongbyon.
Kim justifies nuke program by citing threats from US, South KoreaKim said his latest inspection visit was part of efforts to strengthen North Korea's defense capabilities in response to "variable nuclear threats approaching the Korean Peninsula moment by moment." He accused the U.S. of inciting its regional allies to possess nuclear-powered submarines and committing to sharing its nuclear weapons with them, KCNA said.
"The validity and substantiality of our possession of nuclear weapons and the trend of bolstering up its nuclear capability in quality and quantity are an irreversible reality," Kim said, according to KCNA.
Kim also said the deployment of low-yield battlefield nuclear weapons across multiple domains for various missions is crucial and urgent given North Korea's "inevitable reality facing the border with the most dangerous enemy state," a reference to South Korea. North Korea has in recent years focused on developing such tactical nuclear weapons amid heightened animosity with South Korea.
"Trump has talked about a willingness to meet Kim Jong Un, but the basic U.S. position that North Korea must denuclearize remains unchanged. So Kim Jong Un wants to say 'Look at how powerful we are. title: New UK-EU treaty has 10-year termination clause
summary: Text of the treaties was published this afternoon, alongside legislation designed to enact the bulk of the deal.
text:
New UK-EU treaty has 10-year termination clause
- Published
The government and the EU have published the texts of two treaties agreed last week as part of a post-Brexit reset.
The treaties were published on Thursday afternoon, alongside legislation designed to enact the bulk of the deal.
The deal covering food exports has a 10-year termination clause that would mean if one party ended the agreement, they would have to pay "reasonable and proportionate costs" to rebuild border checks infrastructure, which will be significantly scaled back as part of the new deal.
Opposition leader Kemi Badenoch has said she would scrap the deal while Reform UK's Nigel Farage has suggested he would refuse to pay.
The Brexit reset deal has already sparked debate about its benefits, its costs, and a wider discussion on the future of the UK-EU relationship.
The deal covers British food exports, emissions trading and a youth experience scheme.
Two of the three legal texts were released on Thursday, covering the food trade and emissions trading scheme deals, alongside the government's cost-cutting bill to enact the deal.
A new assessment of the impact of the deal on different sectors and regions of the country was also released.

The industry and government hope the reduction in costs for food producers and sellers will be passed on to customers, but there may be no clear visible impact at the checkout.
Privately, industry insiders told the BBC earlier this week that there are too many moving parts in the world economy, in particular the energy price shock resulting from war in the Middle East.
Regarding the fine detail in the text of one of the treaties relating to the 10-year termination clause, European affairs minister Hamish Falconer said: "The Cutting Costs Bill allows us to implement two major trade agreements."
"It allows us to eliminate paperwork for our food and drink traders, protect billions of pounds worth of British exports from carbon taxes, and make doing business with our largest trading partner cheaper and easier."
A plan to link British and European emissions trading schemes will see more coverage across the UK's aviation and maritime industries.

title: Pregnant US inmate escapes in prison vehicle after medical appointment
summary: Rebecca Taylor had been imprisoned in New Mexico for multiple theft and burglary charges.
text:
Pregnant US inmate escapes in prison vehicle after medical appointment
- Published
A pregnant inmate has escaped from custody in the US state of New Mexico, after taking control of a police vehicle while returning to prison from a prenatal appointment, the state's corrections department has said.
Rebecca Taylor, 26, took control of the Dodge Journey and drove away when the team transporting her and another inmate stopped to pick up food in Albuquerque, local media reported.
The New Mexico Corrections Department said that the vehicle and her prison jumpsuit were later recovered, but Taylor remains on the run.
She had been imprisoned for multiple theft and burglary charges, the department said in a Facebook statement.
Local media reported that another inmate, also travelling back from a prenatal appointment, was able to get out of the car as Taylor took control on Wednesday morning.
The corrections department has said that a multi-agency search for Taylor is under way. The BBC has approached it for an update.
The Albuquerque Journal reported that Taylor is currently in her second trimester of pregnancy. For this reason, she was not restrained during transportation, department spokesperson Brittany Roembach said.
"It is the understanding right now that one officer was with the vehicle but not inside of the vehicle when this occurred," she was quoted as saying.
All prisons in New Mexico went into lockdown following Taylor's escape, but it was lifted at 06:00 on Thursday.
However the prison where she was being held, the Western New Mexico Corrections Facility, will remain on "modified movement", and no visitors are currently allowed.
The public has been told not to approach Rebecca Taylor if they see her, and call police straight away.

title: Diesel tanker carrying up to 7,000 tonnes capsizes near Ibiza, killing one
summary: The possible environmental damage is still being assessed by Spain's sea rescue service.
text:
Diesel tanker carrying up to 7,000 tonnes capsizes near Ibiza, killing one
- Published
An oil tanker carrying up to 7,000 tonnes of diesel has capsized off the coast of Ibiza, leaving one crew member dead, authorities have said.
The Med Emre, a Malta-flagged vessel, was carrying 17 crew members who were all rescued. However seven were taken to hospital and one was later pronounced dead, Balearic Islands emergency services confirmed.
The six crew receiving treatment reportedly suffered minor injuries, such as hypothermia, Spanish media reports.
The possible environmental damage is being assessed by a plane and Spain's pollution control vessel, Clara Campoamor, which is owned by the country's national maritime rescue service.
"There is still little information available about a possible fuel spill," Balearic Islands' President Marga Prohens wrote on X.
Regional emergencies director Pablo Gárriz said the tanker had not completely sunk, as had been originally reported. The vessel remains, however, partially submerged.
That made conditions more favourable for carrying out recovery operations, he said, "as we have gone from the possibility of the vessel being at a depth of 1,000m to a situation that allows operations to be carried out on the surface".
The Med Emre capsized 25 nautical miles (46 km; 29 miles) from Ibiza's coastline and 57 nautical miles from Valencia. It is unclear what caused the sinking.
The chemical tanker was en route from Algeciras, in southern Spain, to Barcelona in the north-east.
Rescuers in Valencia received a distress call around 22:30 local time (21:30 GMT) on Wednesday, according to Spanish media. Minutes later, the vessel reported a leak and the crew said it was leaning at a 90-degree angle.
The injured crew members have been taken to hospitals in Valencia and Can Misses Hospital in Ibiza, President Prohens said.
Ibiza's marine environment was added to the Unesco World Heritage List in 1999. In particular, it is home to dense prairies of Posidonia oceanic seagrass, which is found only in the Mediterranean basin and plays a vital role in supporting local marine biodiversity.
In 2002, Spain experienced one of its worst environmental disasters when the Prestige oil tanker ran into trouble off Galicia's coastline. It spilled more than 60,000 tonnes of heavy fuel oil into the sea.

title: Musk's plan to send a million SpaceX data satellites into space approved
summary: The Starmind constellation aims to be the most cost and energy-efficient way to meet the growing demand for AI computing power.
text:
Musk's plan to send a million SpaceX data satellites into space approved
- Published
US regulators have given SpaceX the go-ahead to launch a million satellites into Earth's orbit to help build data centres in space - the first approval of its kind.
The company, which is owned by Elon Musk, wants to use sunlight to power satellites that will process data for AI and send the results back to Earth.
The Federal Communications Commission (FCC) said on Wednesday that the project, known as Starmind, would "support America's booming super intelligence economy".
However, rival firm Amazon has criticised it as a "lofty ambition rather than a real plan", while astronomers in the US said the move would "significantly undermine" the public's ability to study and observe the night sky.
There is increasing opposition to data centres on earth, including in the US where experts say they were a factor in the Republicans big losses in the midterm elections.
SpaceX believes the "orbital data centres" are the most cost and energy-efficient way to meet the growing demand for artificial intelligence (AI) computing power that is beyond "terrestrial capabilities".
FCC Chairman Brendan Carr said in a statement that the project "opens a bold new frontier for the computing infrastructure needed to power America's leadership and growth".
"This is the kind of American ingenuity that can unite our strengths in space and advanced technology, reinforce our economic leadership, and expand prosperity here at home," Carr said.
Responding to the announcement, Musk wrote on X: "Much appreciated. This will be a great asset to America and the world."

The company has already said it wants to launch its first Starmind satellite next year.
It is unclear whether a million satellites will indeed be launched or whether SpaceX has sought approval for a higher number than it will use.
Like SpaceX's current Starlink network, which provides high-speed internet via more than 10,000 satellites, Starmind's satellites will operate in low-Earth orbit at altitudes ranging between 500-2,000km (310-1,242 miles).
Starmind's satellites will communicate with Starlink's and then relay the data to Earth.

title: At Albuquerque's Indian Pueblo Kitchen, Native American dishes are the main course
summary: At an Albuquerque, N.M., museum, the restaurant is just as much of a draw as the exhibitions, with dishes like green chile stew and sweet biscochitos flavored with anise and cinnamon.
text:
At Albuquerque's Indian Pueblo Kitchen, Native American dishes are the main course
At Albuquerque’s Indian Pueblo Kitchen, Native American dishes are the main course
There are plenty of kitschy diners and barbecue joints along Route 66, but just a couple of miles off the highway in Albuquerque, N.M., Native American dishes are the star at Indian Pueblo Kitchen.
Late on a weekday morning, the restaurant was already starting to fill up. Most of the tables were taken up by locals, like Merlyn Liberty and Rolf Pendall.
"I started with breakfast dessert. The blue corn waffles. And now I'm finishing up my sweetheart's plate of enchiladas and pinto beans," Pendall said.
The restaurant is attached to the Indian Pueblo Cultural Center, a museum and cultural center founded in 1976 by the 19 Pueblo tribes of New Mexico.
The center sits on land where the Albuquerque Indian School operated. Open from 1881 to the early 1980s, it was one of the hundreds of federally funded boarding schools designed to strip Native American children of their family bonds, languages, culture and spiritual practices.
The Indian Pueblo Cultural Center's president and CEO, Monique Fragua, said visitors can start in the museum's galleries and then visit the restaurant to experience Pueblo culture and hospitality.
"Whether that's through our exhibits, or our food, or in our gift shop, we can celebrate the art of our Pueblo communities," Fragua said.
Museum cafés are not a typical destination for foodies, but this one is.
The menu is all Native American and Southwestern-inspired. Dishes include blue corn enchiladas that you can get "Christmas style," one with red chile sauce and the other with green chile sauce. There's a chile posole with beef short ribs served on the bone, as well as Indian tacos on homemade fry bread. Then there's a dish that's really popular on social media: pickles marinated in cherry Kool-Aid and then deep-fried and served with a green chile ranch sauce.
Rita Toledo, from Jemez Pueblo, is Indian Pueblo Kitchen's star baker. One of her specialties is biscochitos — fragrant shortbread cookies spiced with anise and rolled in cinnamon sugar that are New Mexico's state cookie. Toledo has made some twists on the traditional biscochito, like making a chile pepper version that has just a little kick at the end with a nice balance of sweet and heat.
Indian Pueblo Kitchen's version of biscochitos is so popular that the restaurant also sells them at its café inside Albuquerque's airport. Toledo turns out at least 48 dozen biscochitos each week just for the airport location.
While we chatted, Toledo was wrestling to open a giant tub of one of her main ingredients — lard. These cookies can be made with butter or shortening, she said, but "lard's the only way to make good biscochitos."
Toledo said that she has been baking all her life and that her favorite part of her work is rolling out dough.

title: Gérard Depardieu to stand trial for alleged rape of actress in 2018, court rules
summary: A Paris appeals court rules Depardieu will go on trial for the alleged rape of Charlotte Arnould.
text:
Gérard Depardieu to stand trial for alleged rape of actress in 2018, court rules
- Published
French film actor Gérard Depardieu is to stand trial for the alleged rape of actress Charlotte Arnould, a Paris appeals court has confirmed.
Arnould, who was 22 at the time, had reported the alleged rape several days after going to his house in Paris to rehearse a play.
She has waived her right to anonymity and her lawyer said Thursday's ruling was a "first" and the forthcoming trial would be historic.
Depardieu, 77, had contested his indictment on two counts of rape. In a letter published in Le Figaro in 2023, Depardieu strongly denied Arnould's allegations, saying "there was never any coercion or violence between us".
Depardieu was for decades a leading figure in French and international cinema for roles in Green Card, The Man in the Iron Mask and the Asterix films. He was awarded France's Légion d'honneur in 1996.
But in recent years a series of allegations have been made against him over his conduct on film sets and elsewhere in the wake of France's #MeToo movement, known as balance ton porc (call out your pig).
Last year, he was given an 18-month suspended jail term after he was found guilty of sexually assaulting two women on a film set in Paris in May. He was also placed on the sex offenders register and ordered to pay compensation.
He dropped his appeal against the ruling last week and offered "sincere apologies" for his behaviour on the set of director Jean Becker's 2021 film Les Volets Verts (The Green Shutters).
Depardieu had been a friend of Charlotte Arnould's father and on 7 August 2018 she had gone to his home, where much of what happened was captured on the actor's own CCTV.
Arnould's case was initially dismissed for insufficient evidence, but after she filed a civil complaint, a judicial investigation was opened in the summer of 2020.
Speaking outside the Paris appeal court on Thursday, her lawyer Carine Durrieu Diebolt said the ruling was a victory for her client for whom it was "genuinely a relief".
The appeal court said that while Depardieu should stand trial for what took place on that day, he would not be tried for a further alleged rape at a hotel six days later.
Depardieu's lawyer David-Olivier Kaminski told reporters that court had partly ruled in his favour: "As soon as we get the ruling, we will look into the possibility of appealing to the Court of Cassation."
Meanwhile, Depardieu is under a separate investigation alongside French author Michel Houellebecq for "allegations of a sexual nature".
French authorities confirmed their inquiry last week, following reports of an alleged "gang rape" on the set of the film Thalasso in 2018.

title: Alaskan flying team airdrops Thanksgiving turkeys to remote communities

text:
Alaskan flying team airdrops Thanksgiving turkeys to remote communities
For the last few years, "turkey bombers" Esther Keim and Heidi Hastings have taken to the skies to airdrop Thanksgiving turkeys to residents in off-grid communities in south-central Alaska.
Hastings pilots the plane while her best friend Keim drops the turkeys out the plane window, delivering to families who may not otherwise get one of the birds, since they are cut off by snow and ice.

title: 'Memories of a Good Meal': How food made a difference during WWII
summary: New Orleans Chef Alon Shaya's new cookbook shares stories of resilience from World War II, centered around food.
text:
'Memories of a Good Meal': How food made a difference during WWII
NEW ORLEANS — Chef Alon Shaya believes there's power in a meal.
"It's always been the way that I can start a conversation, build a relationship, disagree about things, but still be able to come together and break bread," Shaya, of the acclaimed Crescent City restaurant Saba, said one recent afternoon. "When you share a meal with someone, a lot of those barriers get broken down."
The Israeli American chef also believes food can be a source of inspiration even in the darkest of times. A few years ago, he spearheaded the Rescued Recipes initiative at the United States Holocaust Memorial Museum, and that got him digging deeper into the role that food played during World War II.
Now, he's collected those stories and the dishes they inspired in a new historical cookbook, Memories of a Good Meal: Recipes of Resilience Inspired by Stories of World War II Survival.
Shaya hopes home cooks use the recipes to inspire dinner table conversations about the deeper stories behind them.
"I want people to gather and cook and eat and put their phones down, and share a meal and recount these miraculous stories of survival, resilience and heroism," he told NPR.
Stories like that of Roddie Edmonds, a U.S. Army master sergeant, whose unit was captured in the Battle of the Bulge and imprisoned in a German POW camp. (Edmonds posthumously won the Congressional Medal of Honor earlier this year for his refusal to turn in his Jewish troops to be sent to concentration camps.)
One of the ways Edmonds and his fellow prisoners distracted themselves from the horror of the camp was to talk about the foods that reminded them of home, be it Sunday spaghetti sauce, hot cakes or cherry pie.
"They're eating up this idea that they were going to go home," Shaya said. "They were going to be free, and they were going to be able to sit around and dig into that filet mignon with creamy mushroom sauce."
The servicemen sketched out detailed plans for a dreamed-of restaurant called the Jolly Chef. There, they would serve all those yearned-for dishes, including candied yams with pecans and whipped marshmallow — one of the recipes in the new cookbook.
Another chapter highlights Polish partisan fighters who lived in underground bunkers and sabotaged the Nazis by derailing trains and blowing up ammunition plants. In a nod to the fire that ensued, a recipe from their chapter also includes smashed potatoes flambéed in vodka.
"Vodka was a form of currency for them," Shaya said. "They would use it to barter. They would use it to celebrate. And so each moment of that recipe helps to really tell the story of what they were going through."
The book has stories from around the world – Hungarian Jews whose non-Jewish cook salvaged the treasured family cookbook as they were being sent to Auschwitz; a French village that took in Jewish children and hid them from the Nazis; Navajo code breakers who changed the course of the war; and Japanese Amer

title: Pregnant US inmate escapes in prison vehicle after medical appointment
summary: Rebecca Taylor had been imprisoned in New Mexico for multiple theft and burglary charges.
text:
Pregnant US inmate escapes in prison vehicle after medical appointment
- Published
A pregnant inmate has escaped from custody in the US state of New Mexico, after taking control of a police vehicle while returning to prison from a prenatal appointment, the state's corrections department has said.
Rebecca Taylor, 26, took control of the Dodge Journey and drove away when the team transporting her and another inmate stopped to pick up food in Albuquerque, local media reported.
The New Mexico Corrections Department said that the vehicle and her prison jumpsuit were later recovered, but Taylor remains on the run.
She had been imprisoned for multiple theft and burglary charges, the department said in a Facebook statement.
Local media reported that another inmate, also travelling back from a prenatal appointment, was able to get out of the car as Taylor took control on Wednesday morning.
The corrections department has said that a multi-agency search for Taylor is under way. The BBC has approached it for an update.
The Albuquerque Journal reported that Taylor is currently in her second trimester of pregnancy. For this reason, she was not restrained during transportation, department spokesperson Brittany Roembach said.
"It is the understanding right now that one officer was with the vehicle but not inside of the vehicle when this occurred," she was quoted as saying.
All prisons in New Mexico went into lockdown following Taylor's escape, but it was lifted at 06:00 on Thursday.
However the prison where she was being held, the Western New Mexico Corrections Facility, will remain on "modified movement", and no visitors are currently allowed.
The public has been told not to approach Rebecca Taylor if they see her, and call police straight away.

title: Four-time MVP Rodgers released and may have played last NFL game
summary: Aaron Rodgers is replaced as the Pittsburgh Steelers' starting quarterback, then criticises head coach Mike McCarthy before being released with immediate effect.
text:
Four-time MVP Rodgers released and may have played last NFL game
- Published
Veteran quarterback Aaron Rodgers may have played his last game in the NFL after being released by the Pittsburgh Steelers.
In a brief statement published on Wednesday afternoon local time, the Steelers announced Rodgers, the NFL's four-time Most Valuable Player, was no longer with the franchise.
That came after a tumultuous 24 hours, which began with the Steelers announcing at 23:10 local time on Tuesday that Rodgers had been replaced as their starting quarterback.
He then appeared on US sports TV programme the Pat McAfee Show on Wednesday, saying he would not rejoin the team.
"That ship has sailed," said Rodgers, who turns 43 next week.
During the 34-minute interview, he said he discovered he had been replaced from team-mate Pat Freiermuth.
Rodgers was also critical of Steelers head coach Mike McCarthy, including accusing him of snoring while he slept through team meetings.
They won the Super Bowl together with the Green Bay Packers in 2011 and, during Sunday's loss to the Philadelphia Eagles, Rodgers said that McCarthy ended the half-time huddle with a chant of "one, two, three, Packers".
When asked by reporters on Wednesday about that claim, McCarthy admitted there was "an embarrassing moment".
The 63-year-old was in charge for most of Rodgers' 18-year spell with the Packers and left in 2018. He then coached the Dallas Cowboys from 2020-2024.
Tension had developed between the pair over play-calling and Rodgers said he told McCarthy "try to bench me or don't change the play-caller, then you should just release me".
McCarthy later said "there was an ultimatum made that was clearly outside his job description", adding it was his decision to let the player go.
All this came after the Steelers said that Mason Rudolph will start Friday's home game against the Denver Broncos and that Rodgers would be inactive, so would not serve as back-up to the 31-year-old.
Rodgers, who joined Pittsburgh in 2025 after two years with the New York Jets, was "99% sure" he was going to retire after leading the Steelers to last season's play-offs.
McCarthy's appointment persuaded him to play one more year but Rodgers told the talk show on Wednesday the season had not been "what I signed up for".
Although the Steelers have a 6-4 record, they have had two straight defeats after losing 19-16 at Philadelphia on Sunday.
Analysis - an unceremonious end to an illustrious career?
Pittsburgh's brief statement confirming Rodgers' release, external is likely the unceremonious end to an illustrious career.
While Rodgers was unable to claim a second Super Bowl win with Green Bay, he was named the season MVP in 2011, 2014, 2020 and 2021. Only Peyton Manning (five) has won the award more times.
Rodgers had said his 22nd year in the NFL would be his last, and he has been let go at a crucial stage in the season.

title: A dish with a story, Thanksgiving with culinary historian Michael Twitty
summary: NPR's Leila Fadel welcomes culinary historian Michael Twitty into her kitchen for a Thanksgiving cooking session on making Kush, the forerunner to Southern cornbread dressing.
text:
A dish with a story, Thanksgiving with culinary historian Michael Twitty
Culinary historian Michael Twitty on tracing familial connections through food
This Thanksgiving, Morning Edition host Leila Fadel left the studio for her kitchen, where she was met by the two-time James Beard Award winner Michael Twitty, who came with a spice blend, fresh sage, fish peppers and onions from his garden.
His book, The Cooking Gene, planted him as one of the nation's foremost chronologists tracing his ancestry through African American culinary history.
Kush, the forerunner to Southern cornbread dressing
Kush is one of Twitty's most beloved Thanksgiving offerings and one he's been making since he was a teen. The name and the ingredients show the way food became a tool for the enslaved in the Americas to preserve their cultures.
"The name comes from Hausa, the language of West Africa. They are a predominantly Muslim people, but Muslim in the way that West Africans do Islam – which is Islam with a lot of the influence from the traditional culture and spirituality," he said on the origins of the side dish. "And so the name Kush, it's like, couscous," he added.
The dish is one that connects Twitty to his ancestry.
"There was a time when I couldn't tell you what particular African ethnic groups I came from, but now that I know that I'm part Wolof, Hausa, Fula, and Serer and so many others," he said. "Now, I know this dish has a connection to who I am and my roots and where I came from."
In the making of this dish, Twitty also shared his work documenting the ways African American Jewish people create hybrid dishes in the kitchen.
"It's Matzah ball gumbo, and it's black-eyed peas and quiche," he said of his Black and Jewish identity. "It's a lot of dishes that were from North Africa or from Ethiopia, it's kosher jollof rice and Shito. Shito usually has shellfish in it – we don't put that."
What Thanksgiving and this dish mean to Twitty
The author of four books tracing the deep roots of the foods he loves says for him it's less about the lore of Thanksgiving, and more about the people the day brings together.
"I have to say that along with a lot of other African Americans, not everybody, but a plurality of us, Thanksgiving, as it's been expressed, means very little," he said of the holiday. "Which means we're not attaching ourselves to the myth of Thanksgiving, we don't really care for that. But we do love tradition, we love cooking, we love food, we love gathering."
And in that spirit, Kush in particular, remains one way for him to taste history.
"It means I haven't forgotten who I come from. And it means I haven't forgotten that I have a legacy to leave," he said.
You can find the recipe for Twitty's Kush in his book, Recipes from the American South.

title: Tributes for Duran Duran guitarist Andy Taylor after his death aged 65
summary: Simon Le Bon and his other bandmates say Taylor "brought an indelible fire and swagger to our music".
text:
Tributes for Duran Duran guitarist Andy Taylor after his death aged 65
- Published
Simon Le Bon, Sir Rod Stewart and Gary Kemp are among the pop stars who have paid tribute to Duran Duran guitarist Andy Taylor following his death at the age of 65.
Taylor co-wrote some of the group's biggest hits including Save A Prayer, Rio and Girls On Film.
Le Bon and his bandmates paid tribute, saying "he brought an indelible fire and swagger to our music", while Sir Rod remembered his "dear pal" and Spandau Ballet's Kemp called him "a great player who set the tone for the 80s".
Taylor's wife Tracey called him "the rock of our family", adding: "We will miss him every single day." He died after "a long and courageous battle with prostate cancer", Duran Duran said in a statement on Wednesday.
- Andy Taylor: Duran Duran's livewire guitarist who was a Wild Boy on stage and off 
  - Published21 hours ago
He died "peacefully at home, surrounded by his family, on Monday 23rd November", a statement said.
Paying tribute, his Duran Duran bandmates said: "From the moment he arrived in Birmingham from the North East with a guitar and an unshakeable belief in what we could become, he brought an indelible fire and swagger to our music.
"His playing drove the songs that took us around the world, and with a dry wit that was matched only by his wonderfully unsentimental, no-nonsense outlook on life he kept us grounded and gave the band its edge through the extraordinary years that followed."
They said their thoughts were with his wife, children and grandson.
Le Bon said there was a "a massive Andy Taylor shaped hole in my heart".
"Andy never took the easy musical route. His overdrive overdrove us into being the only funk/rock/punk band in the New Romantic movement, with songs that still survive, decades later."
Sir Rod, who wrote five songs with Taylor for the 1988 album Out of Order, recalled them making "some good music together" and having "some outrageous fun".
Kemp said Taylor "influenced many of us along the way with his sparse staccato style", adding: "He brought shameless rock to the mix."
In a band tribute, Spandau Ballet called him "a hugely talented musician and an important part of the British music scene".
US guitarist Nile Rodgers, the co-founder of Chic, recalled "countless great days and nights" with his "dear friend".
Belinda Carlisle said she was "blessed" to have worked with Taylor, who played the guitar solo and was in the video for her song Mad About You.
Former Led Zeppelin frontman Robert Plant called Taylor "a tough fighter", while Then Jerico's Mark Shaw remembered him as "one of the greatest musicians and songwriters I've ever heard and had the privilege to work with".
Taylor's wife Tracey, a hairstylist he met during the early days of Duran Duran, and whom he married in 1982, said: "For all the incredible experiences music brought him, family always came first for Taylor, adding: "Nothing made him happier than having us all together."

title: FedEx plane sends dirt flying while overshooting Miami runway
summary: An aircraft overran a runway at Miami International Airport in Florida on Wednesday leading to a halt in flights.
text:
FedEx plane sends dirt flying while overshooting Miami runway
A FedEx aircraft overran a runway at Miami International Airport in Florida on Wednesday leading to a halt in flights.
No injuries were reported and the Federal Aviation Administration is investigating the incident.
The ground stop comes on the day before Thanksgiving, one of the busiest travel days of the year in the US.

title: Court lets Puerto Rico governor fire firm that runs the island's troubled power grid
summary: LUMA Energy took over the electric grid five years ago. The court's ruling nullifies its contract, and gives the government a year to find a new operator.
text:
Court lets Puerto Rico governor fire firm that runs the island's troubled power grid
Puerto Rico Supreme Court allows governor to fire company that runs the island's troubled power grid
LUMA Energy took over the electric grid five years ago. The court's ruling nullifies its contract, and gives the government a year to find a new operator.
A MARTÍNEZ, HOST:
Puerto Rico's supreme court has ruled the island's governor can kick out the private company that's been running its troubled power grid for five years. The decision could have huge consequences for electric service in Puerto Rico. Here is NPR's Adrian Florido.
ADRIAN FLORIDO, BYLINE: After Hurricane Maria flattened Puerto Rico's already rickety power grid in 2017, the island's government privatized it. It gave a company called LUMA Energy, based in Canada and Texas, a 15-year deal to take over the power lines, promising that LUMA would rebuild the grid stronger and improve the notoriously unreliable service. LUMA took over in 2021. But things have not gone as planned.
Blackouts are still a constant fact of life. LUMA has come in for harsh criticism from customers and officials. Last year, Governor Jenniffer Gonzalez-Colon filed suit to nullify LUMA's contract. Yesterday, the Puerto Rican Supreme Court ruled in her favor that LUMA must go.
(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)
JENNIFFER GONZALEZ-COLON: Today is a day of celebration on the island.
FLORIDO: This is the governor speaking after the ruling. She said LUMA has not lived up to its promises.
(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)
GONZALEZ-COLON: More outages on the island, more shutdowns on the island. They have not fulfilled the requirements of the contract.
FLORIDO: In fact, the island's supreme court ruled on procedural grounds, saying officials had not followed local requirements when approving agreements with the company. The court gave the local government a year to put a new operator in place. The governor said the work to find a new private company will start immediately.
(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)
GONZALEZ-COLON: It's going to be a good transition. We're going to make it in a year. And I hope that all companies that are interested in participating in this process will fulfill and follow the process of law. And we're going to be opening that process for public bid.
FLORIDO: The court gave LUMA Energy 10 days to request a reconsideration of its ruling. In a statement, LUMA said it is considering its legal options. The company has long argued that the grid it took over was in awful shape and that it is not fully to blame for the blackouts. A new operator will need approval from both the local government and a federal oversight board that Congress put in place 10 years ago to get Puerto Rico out of bankruptcy. title: Egyptian authorities arrest motorist over tanker crash that killed 31
summary: Officials say the man confessed to travelling at speed and clipping the fuel truck as he was overtaking traffic.
text:
Egyptian authorities arrest motorist over tanker crash that killed 31
- Published
Egyptian authorities have arrested a man accused of causing a tanker crash and massive fire that killed 31 people on a busy Cairo highway.
The public prosecutor's office said the motorist had confessed to driving at 110km/h (68mph) along a section of ring road, to the north of the old city centre, and clipping the tanker with the side of his car as he changed lanes.
Sources close to the investigation were earlier quoted by state media as saying a high-voltage cable had fallen in front of the fuel truck, causing the driver to lose control.
Twenty-one others were injured in the crash in the Warraq neighbourhood on Wednesday evening, with hospitals treating patients for burns and smoke inhalation.
The public prosecutor's office said on Thursday that "upon questioning the suspect and confronting him with the findings of the investigation... he confessed to committing the act".
"He added that, while moving between traffic lanes and overtaking vehicles, the left side of his car collided with the right rear side of the tanker. This caused him to lose control of the steering wheel and his car veered to the far right of the road."
At the same time, one of the fuel tanker's tyres burst, causing it to veer into the highway's central reservation, hit the concrete barrier and overturn, spilling fuel and igniting a fire, the prosecutor's office said.
Egyptian authorities have not named the suspect accused of causing the fatal crash, but they said he had been travelling with his father at the time.
The raised motorway - a major artery for traffic around the Egyptian capital - was reopened by emergency services hours after the crash occurred, with the burnt-out wrecks of cars shifted to the side by bulldozers and diggers.
A cabinet minister said on Thursday that 10 million Egyptian pounds (£139,000; $182,000) had been donated to the families of the victims, while the nation's sports minister said all state-run celebratory activities would be cancelled in the aftermath of the crash.
Egypt has suffered several deadly fires in recent years. Road collisions are also common, attributed to poor maintenance and violations of traffic laws, and leading to thousands of road deaths a year.

title: Macy's postpones Thanksgiving parade due to severe weather
summary: The move represents the first postponement of the iconic event, and comes after a forecast of strong winds and heavy rain.
text:
Macy's postpones Thanksgiving parade due to severe weather
- Published
Macy's has postponed its 100th annual Thanksgiving Day Parade in New York to Saturday because of severe weather.
Preparations to hold the iconic holiday celebration, known for its massive balloons that float among the city's skyscrapers, had already begun when the forecast for heavy rain and strong winds on Thursday led to the delay.
The parade was suspended was during World War Two, but it has never before been postponed due to weather. In 1971, Macy's decided to ground the balloons, which often feature beloved characters from pop culture, because of weather.
A powerful coastal storm is set to affect the New York area in coming days.
On Wednesday night, New York Governor Kathy Hochul declared a state of emergency for Long Island, New York City and Westchester County.
The potent nor'easter is expected to make it too windy and dangerous for the iconic balloons to fly.
Macy's had expected to put 100 inflatables into the sky to mark its 100th parade and feature 10 new balloons, including one depicting the animated dog Bluey wearing a crown and another showing a Minion character riding a banana like a horse.
"While we are heartbroken that our parade was postponed, the safety of our partners, the safety of our participants and spectators is, and always will be, our top priority," said Will Cross, the parade's executive producer, during a news conference on Wednesday with city officials.
Cross also said the giant balloons would be deflated on Wednesday night and stored at a facility in neighbouring New Jersey until they were reinflated for the parade on Saturday.
Macy's confirmed the new parade date and updated a countdown clock on its website to reflect the Saturday schedule. Meanwhile, broadcaster NBC has said it will show the 2025 parade on Thursday.
New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani, who will not attend the parade on Saturday because of a scheduled surgery, said at the news conference that "you have to plan for every possibility" and confirmed that "extreme weather has forced" officials to make the change.
"We know that this is an inconvenience for many who come to visit our city. This decision, however, was made with safety being paramount," he said. "We want to ensure that we're delivering a parade that's not only incredible and spectacular, but one also that doesn't come at the expense of anyone's safety."
Mamdani also said that there would be an expanded police presence along the parade route on Saturday and that there were "no known specific or credible threats to the parade at this time".
Cross added that Macy's is working through what costs it could cover as a result of the delay and said the company is in contact with bands, performers and others who travelled to the city for the parade.
During some past parades, strong winds and inclement weather have led to the tearing and deflation of the balloons as well as collisions with lampposts that caused injuries.

title: Powerful storms disrupt holiday travel, as Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade is postponed
summary: Extreme weather that has unleashed strong winds, high tides, heavy rain and floods is expected to impact travel plans of an estimated 81.5 million people as they travel across the United States.
text:
Powerful storms disrupt holiday travel, as Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade is postponed
Storms expected on both coasts as millions travel for Thanksgiving
Tens of millions of people are bracing for delays at airports and highways across the country on Thursday, as powerful storms across the United States threatened to disrupt travel for the Thanksgiving holiday.
On the West Coast, high tides have flooded streets along California's shorelines and knocked off a part of Pacifica Pier. The floods have also prompted evacuation warnings. On the East Coast, authorities are preparing to weather the impact of a storm making its way up into New England from the southeast with strong winds and heavy rain. Snow was also forecast in parts of the Midwest.
Some 81.5 million people in the U.S. are expected to travel for the holiday between Thursday and Monday, according to AAA.
Hundreds of flights had already been cancelled or delayed by early morning Thursday, particularly on the East Coast, where authorities have warned people to stay home as the storm barrels through. The majority of people are expected to travel by car for the holidays, and the winter weather could affect their plans due to visibility issues on the road.
Richard Bann, a meteorologist with the National Weather Service Weather Prediction Center, told NPR that the East Coast storm remained the main concern, calling it a "multi-hazard" storm.
"It's going to be getting better organized as we go through the day, and it'll be spreading a considerable amount of wind, heavy rain. The real concern with this thing is going to be coastal flooding," Bann said.
Meteorologist Matthew Cappucci with The Washington Post and MyRadar told NPR the storm's magnitude at this time of the year was "unusual."
"We would expect this in deep winter," Cappucci said.
The storm in the East Coast, however, is expected to mostly clear out by Saturday, easing weekend travel for those returning from Thanksgiving gatherings.
Macy's Thanksgiving Day parade in New York City delayed
Beyond travel, several Thanksgiving parades have also been affected by severe weather.
The incoming storm is expected to cause high winds in New York City, prompting Mayor Zohran Mamdani on Wednesday to delay the city's famous Macy's Thanksgiving Day parade. Organizers were already inflating the iconic giant balloons for the parade on Wednesday when officials announced the decision.
The parade, which is now expected to take place on Saturday, will be the city's 100th, and while it was cancelled before during World War II, this is the first time that it's been postponed in the last century.
The parade's organizers said it took two years to prepare the elaborate celebration, which includes over 11,000 participants and volunteers, thousands of high school marching band musicians from across the country and hundreds of balloon handlers. In previous years, up to 2 million spectators have attended the parade.
